entry.title: Public-sector banks need autonomy and professional governance to compete
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Public-sector banks need autonomy and professional governance to competePublic-sector banks need autonomy and professional governance to compete

The absence of "phone banking" today offers no institutional guarantee against its return. Stronger PSB balance sheets offer an opportunity to reform from a position of strength

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ananth Narayan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:22 PM ISTThe government has constituted a High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat. It will review the sector’s legal and regulatory framework, prudential norms and capital needs, and chart a path to globally competitive Indian banks. Its terms of reference do not explicitly mention public-sector bank (PSB) governance. Yet, it cannot sidestep how a substantial part of Indian banking is owned and run.  Past committees and their recommendations  The Narasimham committees of 1991 and 1998 recommended greater operational autonomy for PSBs, professional boards and management, freedom from political and administrative interference, and a more competitive banking ecosystem. They sought to end dual control by the finance ministry and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), giving primacy to the latter. Narasimham II also proposed that government ownership be reduced to 33 per cent.  The P J Nayak committee of 2014 proposed transferring government shareholdings to a professionally managed Bank Investment Company, bringing PSBs under the Companies Act instead of their special governing statutes, and empowering bank boards to appoint management, determine remuneration, and oversee performance. It also sought ownership-neutral RBI regulation.  These recommendations emerged in difficult circumstances. Narasimham I followed the 1991 economic crisis. Narasimham II came amid persistent weaknesses in asset quality. In 2014, another wave of stressed PSB loans had built up, though yet to be recognised.  PSBs — healthier and socially relevant  Today, PSBs are considerably healthier. Average price-to-book ratios of large PSBs have risen from around 0.6 in the late 2010s to 1 in recent years. Their return on equity, negative for much of the previous decade, has recovered to 15 per cent.  But this follows an expensive clean-up. Between FY10 and FY25, PSBs, including IDBI Bank, wrote off around ₹13.6 trillion of loans. Writeoffs do not necessarily represent final losses, since recoveries can follow. Between FY13 and FY22, the government infused ₹3.75 trillion into PSBs, including IDBI.  This does not mean that government ownership is undesirable. An August 2022 study by RBI economists in their personal capacity found that while private banks were more profit-efficient, PSBs performed better on financial inclusion, and their lending was less procyclical.  PSBs remain central to financial inclusion. Their share of overall scheduled commercial bank deposits has fallen from around 75 per cent in 2011 to below 60 per cent. Yet they still hold over 80 per cent of rural deposits and around 70 per cent in semi-urban areas. They remain important providers of micro, small and medium enterprises credit.  The government’s developmental objectives are important. However, where the government seeks outcomes beyond obligations applicable to all banks, explicit guarantees, interest subsidies or viability-gap support could be offered to both public and private lenders alike. Any costs should appear in the Budget, rather than being absorbed through PSB cross-subsidies or lower returns.  Public ownership and professional management  In addition, public ownership does not confer banking expertise or justify combining the roles of shareholder, manager, and supervisor.  According to its annual report, the finance ministry’s Department of Financial Services (DFS) handles PSB chief executive and whole-time director appointments, their remuneration and service conditions, analysis of operating results, scrutiny of and follow-up action on RBI’s inspections of PSBs, monitoring of bad loans and recoveries, and responsibilities concerning auditors. While some shareholder oversight is legitimate, many of these functions would ordinarily rest primarily with bank boards, management or the banking regulator.  This creates an uneven playing field. PSB boards have a limited role in senior appointments and pay. In FY26, the remuneration of chief executives at the three largest private banks was 15-30 times that of their counterparts at large PSBs, even before accounting for some equity-linked incentives. PSB chiefs also typically have shorter tenures, limiting continuity in leadership and strategy, a concern also flagged by the Nayak committee.  Regulatory powers are asymmetric. The RBI lacks certain statutory powers available over private banks, including those relating to PSB management removal and board supersession. In March 2018, then RBI Governor Urjit Patel argued that banking regulatory powers should be ownership-neutral.  DFS is staffed by capable civil servants, but senior officials rotate across government assignments. Overseeing complex banks demands sustained expertise in credit, risk, capital and strategy. A professionally managed institution and board with dedicated banking expertise may be better placed to discharge these responsibilities, with less political and administrative influence.  International experience  International experience offers lessons, but no ready template. Singapore’s Temasek owns 28 per cent of DBS, leaving commercial decisions to its professional board and management, while the Monetary Authority of Singapore regulates the bank. Britain placed its peak 84 per cent RBS (NatWest) stake under an arm’s-length ownership agency and reduced its holdings over time. OECD guidelines advocate professional ownership, merit-based boards, and separation of ownership from regulation.  There are cautionary examples too. German savings banks have substantial political involvement in governance, and research documents political influences on lending. Several Landesbanken (regional state-owned banks) separately required rescues after 2008. Brazilian public banks have experienced repeated government support. China's Central Huijin demonstrates that a holding company can come with extensive political control.  India needs a model suited to its circumstances. But how the state owns banks matters as much as whether it owns them. A professional government ownership entity must have credible independence, with bank boards controlling strategy, executive appointments and remuneration. RBI regulation should be ownership-neutral. Creating another bureaucratic layer without transferring real authority would accomplish little.  Awaiting the 1991 moment  The absence of “phone banking” today offers no institutional guarantee against its return. Stronger PSB balance sheets offer an opportunity to reform from a position of strength.  The 1991 reforms dismantled the Licence Raj and marked a break from the idea that government should occupy the commanding heights of the economy, direct businesses, and allocate capital. Banking needs its 1991 moment, separating government ownership from operational control. That requires political leaders and administrators willing to relinquish authority.  Ultimately, PSBs should compete on a level playing field, with minimum government and maximum governance, accountable to their boards and all shareholders, and subject to RBI supervision.

entry.title: RBI may need tighter monetary policy to contain persistent inflation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI may need tighter monetary policy to contain persistent inflationRBI may need tighter monetary policy to contain persistent inflation

Its decision to look through successive supply shocks could prove costly

premium

Rajeswari Sengupta5 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:46 PM ISTIndia’s retail inflation rose to 6.09 per cent in October, crossing the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India’s tolerance band for the first time in two years. This wasn’t unexpected. Over the last few months, food prices have been going up, energy costs have increased and inflationary pressures have been getting more generalised, beyond just food and energy. The RBI’s response so far has been one repo rate hike of 25 basis points in October. It is worth asking, has the RBI fallen behind the curve?  Let’s review the facts first. Inflation did not jump overnight. It has been steadily rising since January and crossed the RBI’s 4 per cent target in June. Core inflation, which leaves out food and fuel, has also been going up. It has increased from 3.3 per cent in January to 4.6 per cent in October. According to the latest data, inflation rose in 11 of the 12 groups of the consumer price index. The pressure is no longer limited to a few items.  Three factors are responsible for this.  First, food inflation has more than doubled from 4 per cent in April to 8.5 per cent in October. El Nino conditions meant that India received only 87 per cent of its long-term average rainfall during the June-September monsoon season, the lowest since 2015. Deficient rainfall has affected the kharif (summer) crop and also the reservoir levels, raising concerns about the ongoing rabi (winter) crop output too.  Second, the war in West Asia has pushed up prices of crude oil and gas. The Indian government raised petrol and diesel prices by about 8 per cent. Prices of commercial LPG and other inputs such as chemicals and plastics went up by more. Wholesale inflation averaged 10.4 per cent in the July-September quarter. Over time, firms pass on higher input costs to consumers. Higher energy prices also pushed up transport inflation from nearly 0 per cent in April to 5.8 per cent in October.  Third, there is a demand dimension.  If official data is to be believed, real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 7.8 per cent in April-June. Non-food bank credit grew at a staggering rate of 19 per cent in September. Personal loans from banks grew 17.3 per cent, against 11.5 per cent a year ago while retail loans from non-banking finance companies (NBFCs) grew 21.9 per cent. Households are borrowing to spend. This suggests that we have an economy that is growing at close to 8 per cent, where credit-fuelled consumption is pushing up demand, and that has faced two supply shocks in one year — an energy shock and a food shock.  Now let’s look at the RBI’s monetary policy conduct against this background.  These risks were visible well before October. The RBI itself flagged the oil shock and the El Niño risk in its April policy. But it kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent in its April, June and August meetings. It raised the rate to 5.5 per cent in October. That hike only reversed the cut of December 2025.  In fact, in its August meeting, the RBI lowered its inflation forecast for the year to 5 per cent, even though inflation was rising every month. The August meeting was interesting for another reason. The minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee meeting revealed that some members were concerned about persistent inflationary pressures, strong credit growth and rising inflation expectations of households. But, the monetary policy statement published by the RBI came across as more dovish. This suggests that the RBI did not give sufficient weight to the possibility that persistent food and energy shocks would spread to other prices.  The result is that with a repo rate of 5.5 per cent and a headline CPI inflation of 6.09 per cent, the real rate is roughly -0.6 per cent. This means that monetary policy needs to be sufficiently more contractionary in order to bring inflation down to the target level of 4 per cent.  The RBI’s reasoning may be that supply shocks are temporary and a central bank should look through them. This holds when it is a one-time shock, demand is weak and expectations are stable. It is harder to defend when two supply shocks come together, growth is strong, credit is growing at 19 per cent and core inflation is rising. In such conditions, supply shocks spread to wages and other prices. While monetary policy cannot produce more rainfall or lower global oil prices, it can play a crucial role in preventing a supply shock from becoming a persistent inflation problem.  Why does this matter? It matters because inflation is a tax on households. It hurts the poor and the middle class the most. The inflation targeting framework was adopted in 2016 to avoid such episodes. Also, there is a cost to waiting. Once households start revising their inflation expectations upwards, bringing inflation down becomes harder. The RBI may now have to raise rates by more, and keep them higher for longer, to lower both inflation and inflation expectations but at a greater cost to growth.  Hopefully, the central bank would take decisive action going forward to halt the steady rise in inflation and bring it back to the 4 per cent target.  
The writer is associate professor of economics, Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, Mumbai     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Abolish B schools vs pivot B schools? Time to focus on entrepreneurship
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Abolish B schools vs pivot B schools? Time to focus on entrepreneurshipAbolish B schools vs pivot B schools? Time to focus on entrepreneurship

Rather than shutting down, Indian B-schools must pivot from producing corporate talent to nurturing entrepreneurs and future business leaders

premium

Students attending a management class at a business school in India

Ambi Parameswaran5 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:34 PM ISTEver since the article with a sensational title “Should we shut down B Schools” appeared in The New York Times, there has been renewed debate about all that is wrong with business school education. The article was written by Chris Marquis of Cambridge University’s Judge Business School. Marquis has over two decades of experience as a tenured B School professor. If he is calling for a ‘shut down’, there must be some truth to his argument, feel a lot of people.   In India, too, there has been a debate around B schools. Tulsi Jayakumar, a professor at SPJIMR (S P Jain Institute of Management and Research) has argued in her op-ed piece in The Times Of India (November 13, 2026) that Indian B schools are caught in a trap of placement and rankings. Rankings are driven by research and a lot of the research output stays in an echo chamber. The case-method of education pioneered by the Harvard Business School (borrowing the idea from the Harvard Law School, if I may add) has also come in for criticism.   One of the big complaints by Marquis is that B Schools are producing graduates who are single mindedly focused on profit maximisation. And repaying their own student loans. The preferred job options are in consulting and financial services. Very few enter the manufacturing or services sector, even fewer the non-profit sector. The need to bring a stronger societal-well-being focus was also one of the arguments that we have read in the book Rethinking The MBA  (2010, Harvard Business Review Press) written by Srikant Datar, David Garvin and Patrick Cullen.   Let us now switch tracks and look at the Indian scenario. We have over 5,000-plus B schools in India. All B schools that fall below the 200-ranking mark, whichever ranking you may take, are struggling. Enrollments are a challenge. And placements are a bigger challenge. For the top ten or so schools the scenario that was presented by Marquis is similar. Students prefer to join consulting or financial services.   I discussed this with a few students whom I had lunch with before my session at a leading B school just before Diwali. They were curious to know how I jumped into a relatively unknown sector (advertising) after my Indian Institute of Management (IIM)  education.  Was it just foolhardiness or did I really think that through?   I explained that my reason was simple. I had done a summer internship with the ad agency and thought they offered a great learning environment. While the salary was not great, I knew that I would be able to get a significant jump if I proved my mettle. Also as an MBA from a leading business school I was quite sure that I would be able to pivot after a year or two.   How about them? Why this craze to chase the biggest pay packet? Their argument was that many of their friends had big student loans to clear. The easy route to clear those loans was to grab the biggest pay packet. They felt that many of their friends will jump out in two or three years; to head to a sector that interests them. What could they be? A start-up that can help them on their own entrepreneurial journey, was the answer.   That got me thinking.   In 1979 I  joined an ad agency that was started by two MBA graduates, one from Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad (IIMA) and one from Indian Institute of Management  Calcutta (IIMC). It was a start-up, although you may not have used the term then.   And later in my career I went back into advertising, after a nine-year stint in marketing/sales. My entry into advertising was also in a quasi-entrepreneurial role. I was part of a team of five MBAs who came together to turn around an ailing ad agency. It was as entrepreneurial as you can get. We did succeed in saving jobs and turning the agency around; we even managed to find a global buyer for an agency that was said to be on its deathbed just a decade earlier.   This leads me to an argument that is missing from all these ‘shut down B school’ sloganeering. In a country like India we need new companies with growth ambitions. B schools are tailor-made to teach young bright students how to set up and run a business. No other form of education — Bachelor of Commerce (B Com), engineering, Chartered Accountant (CA) or law — comes close.   B schools need to pivot. From being providers of talent to consultancies and financial service majors to creators of future entrepreneurs. Towards this end they should add new courses, new programmes. For example the family managed business programmes offered by several B schools serve a great cause. They try and teach the future inheritors the way to grow their businesses. Then there are online MBA programmes that attract young leaders who are building their own businesses.   As Jayakumar has said in her article, B schools should track their alumni through their career journey. Maybe bring them back for refreshers. Find out how many of them are in entrepreneurial roles or quasi-entrepreneurial roles. There is no point in condemning the craze for consulting or financial services. They pay the most, so let them get the choicest of candidates. But tracking the alumni in a systematic way will definitely help the B school serve the larger cause.   So instead of shutting down B schools, we should ask them to use a term popularised by start-ups: Pivot. By becoming schools for entrepreneurs.  
The writer is an adjunct professor of marketing at SPJIMR, a  best-selling author and founder of Brand-Building.com, a brand advisory   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Higher money growth does not translate into higher inflation in India
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Higher money growth does not translate into higher inflation in IndiaHigher money growth does not translate into higher inflation in India

Rising money supply does not pose an immediate inflation risk, as deposit growth, changing banking patterns and digital payments have altered India's money multiplier, argues the author

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Soumya Kanti Ghosh6 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:21 PM ISTIndia’s monetary aggregates have expanded noticeably in recent months, with broad money (M3) recording year-on-year (Y-o-Y) growth of around 16.5 per cent as of October 2026, while reserve money (M0) reached a record ₹54.02 trillion with a Y-o-Y growth of 11.8 per cent, due to the 100 basis point (bps) reduction in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) in 2025. Several researchers have flagged the acceleration in M3 growth as a source of potential macroeconomic concern, particularly because sustained monetary expansion significantly more than nominal output growth can eventually generate inflationary and asset-price pressures. In my assessment, the current increase does not pose a material risk to the economy at this juncture.  The growth in M3 and M0 has been driven by a rise in currency in circulation, which has increased to  ₹43.6 trillion and an increase in time deposits of banks by 17.6 per cent, led by Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) or FCNR (B) deposits.   Firstly, the increase in currency in circulation is mostly due to an increase in small denomination notes. In fact, I estimate that an around ₹4 trillion of additional cash is floating in the system on account of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) regulation in April 2025 that has mandated that 90 per cent of all ATMs will dispense notes of smaller denominations, like ₹100 and ₹200. Secondly, banks have received around $143.5 billion, of which $132.9 billion is through FCNR(B) deposits, $5.3 billion through Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings (OFCBs) and $5.2 billion through External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs). So, this has increased time deposits around 2x on an incremental basis, which is not an issue for the banks, as the credit growth remains robust. Thus, robust deposit creation alongside strong credit expansion has contributed to the faster growth in broad money.  In fact, the high M3 growth by itself does not necessarily imply an imminent inflation problem. The rise needs to be viewed in the context of strong credit growth, deposit mobilisation, financial deepening and the expansion of the formal financial system, rather than interpreted mechanically as excess monetary accommodation. Moreover, historical experience provides useful perspective: In FY13, when FCNR(B) was mobilised, M3 growth was 13.6 per cent in 2012-13 and 13.4 per cent in 2013-14, while reserve-money growth accelerated from 6.2 per cent to 14.4 per cent over the same period. Thus, the key issue is not the headline M3 growth rate per se, but whether monetary expansion becomes persistently disconnected from underlying nominal economic activity and translates into broad-based inflationary pressures.  In this regard, I would also like to emphasise the role of the textbook money multiplier, the link between M0 and M3. The money multiplier increased to 6.25 end-October 2026, from 6.15 in end-March 2026, propelled by a declining currency-deposit ratio. However, this is not the correct multiplier in the Indian context. I want to highlight three factors that have significantly dampened the money multiplier in India and hence the ability to create deposits by banks through the familiar multiplier route.    First, the change in the structure of deposits from retail to institutional. The ownership (households, governments, and corporations) structure of bank deposits is changing. Households (HH) remain the largest depositors, but their share is gradually declining as they diversify into mutual funds, equities, and other instruments. This results in deposits being counted under financial institutions. This shifting of HHs/retail deposits towards financial institution (FI) deposits has important regulatory implications through run-off factors (as FI deposits attract 100 per cent run-off factor as compared with  merely 5-10 per cent in case of retail deposits). This change in the deposit structure ultimately increases the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirements and lowers the money multiplier and hence the ability of the bank to create deposits. However, effective from 1 April 2026, with the RBI’s revised LCR guidelines, the LCR of banks has increased to 126.74 in June from 124.2 in March 2026.   Second, the impact of the implementation of SNA-SPARSH (Samyochit Pranali Ekikrit Shighra Hastantaran), which is a digital public financial management system introduced by the government to reform how funds flow for centrally sponsored schemes (CSS). Instead of the old system where the Central government gave large advance installments, SNA-SPARSH operates on a “just-in-time” (JIT) release principle. More than 50 CSS have been notified under the SNA-SPARSH.   Due to these, large balances have fully shifted out of commercial banks and has eroded the system’s low-cost current account savings account (Casa) deposits. As per RBI data, both central and state government deposits in the banks have declined by 9 per cent (₹1.5 trillion) in FY26, compared with FY25. Casa deposits have declined by ₹94,385 crore. This phenomenon also lowers the money multiplier and thereby the ability of the banks to create deposits.     Third, the incessant rise in UPI. The UPI reduces the desire of the public to hold cash and keep deposits to make transactions. Thus, a rise in UPI should reduce the money multiplier. My underlying hypothesis is that digital payments substitute cash transactions and therefore reduce the demand for currency held by the public and hence also lowers the money multiplier and thereby deposit creation.   Cumulatively, due to the above three factors, estimation shows that the operating money multiplier in India is around 3.26 — almost half as compared with the textbook multiplier. This implies that the deposit creation capacity of banks is now actually half. For every ₹1, instead of ₹6.25 deposit being created through the multiplier, we are creating ₹3.26.    To sum up, the RBI has been very conscious of monetary management post inflation targeting. The RBI is also currently responding decisively with rate and liquidity management with the inflation outlook warranting such restraint. In an inflation targeting regime, money supply is always endogenous. For the record, average money supply growth for the decade ended FY26 was 10.3 per cent and decisively lagged the nominal gross domestic product growth at 11.3 per cent for the same period.

entry.title: Short covering and foreign inflows are fuelling Indian stock market rebound
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Short covering and foreign inflows are fuelling Indian stock market reboundShort covering and foreign inflows are fuelling Indian stock market rebound

In the three weeks to November 13, the Nifty 50 surged 11.3 per cent, from 22,600 to 25,144, with almost all the gains concentrated in a single spectacular week

premium

Investors who had sold futures had to buy them back, adding demand just as cash-market buying gathered pace (Representative Image)

Debashis Basu5 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 11:49 PM ISTFor much of 2025 and 2026, India’s stock market had an awkward problem: The economy was growing, corporate earnings were improving, yet foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) were heading for the exits. Earlier, India was the emerging market that global investors worried about not owning. For two years, it was the one they could do without. In Bank of America’s Asia Fund Manager Survey, India was the least preferred Asian stock market, with the absence of a clear artificial-intelligence (AI) opportunity as the biggest concern, followed by weak growth, high valuations, and insufficient reform. Newspaper editorials were amplifying the alarm, asking policymakers to heed the warning. The pessimism was overdone. As I mentioned in August this year, the underlying reality was far from alarming. In late October, the tide turned dramatically.  In the three weeks to November 13, the Nifty 50 surged 11.3 per cent, from 22,600 to 25,144, with almost all the gains concentrated in a single spectacular week. Between October 30 and November 6, the benchmark rose 8.6 per cent, its strongest weekly performance in roughly six years. Five forces converged. One, the government hinted that it would consider removing the main irritant for FPIs — long-term capital gains tax. Two, the unwinding of the crowded AI trade in other Asian markets encouraged FPIs to diversify towards India. Three, a sharp fall in prices of crude oil improved India’s external economic prospects. Four, by late October, FPIs had built huge bearish positions in index futures. The rally triggered by FPI buying was turbocharged by powerful short-covering. Five, better corporate earnings provided fundamental support. After months of selling, overseas investors bought Indian equities worth $6.43 billion up to November 12, their biggest monthly purchase in more than two years.  Of the five reasons, the global retreat from the AI trade is the most amusing. In my piece in August, I had argued that the biggest reason to ignore the FPI griping was that India’s listed stocks had little exposure to the current AI mania. That gripe ignored the fact that only Taiwan and South Korea, among countries outside the United States and China, could offer significant exposure to the AI fashion. I had said that no policymaker should lose sleep over this. It would be akin to shunning a country in 1999 because it did not have loss-making listed internet companies, or in 2007 because it did not have financial stocks minting money from toxic subprime mortgages. From the second week of October, American AI stocks, semiconductor makers in Taiwan and South Korea, and suppliers of data-centre infrastructure began a deep dive as investors started to question whether these represented an expensive wager on returns that had yet to materialise. In October, foreigners withdrew nearly $50 billion from seven Asian equity markets, much of it from Taiwan and South Korea. India, with little exposure to the semiconductor supply chain, became a destination for investors seeking diversification.  Meanwhile, Brent crude, which approached $113 a barrel on October 30, fell by about a fifth from its peak before trading near $92 on November 12. The decline reflected reduced fears of further escalation in the Iran conflict and hopes of de-escalation after America’s midterm elections. For India, which imports close to 90 per cent of its oil, the benefits are immediate: A smaller import bill, less pressure on the current account and the rupee, and lower imported inflation. The rupee strengthened by about 1.1 per cent in the week to November 6, its best weekly performance since April. A firm currency makes Indian assets less risky for dollar-based investors, creates a virtuous circle of lower oil prices, a steadier rupee, and renewed inflows. The markets were pricing in a greater chance of deescalation, not settled peace.  The speed of the advance owed much to the unusually large bearish FPI position in Nifty futures, with net shorts estimated at around 280,000 contracts near October 23. Once the index rose, those bets became costly. Investors who had sold futures had to buy them back, adding demand just as cash-market buying gathered pace. By November 6, net shorts had fallen to about 100,000 contracts and Nifty futures open interest had dropped by roughly 22 per cent. Foreign investors were also net buyers of about ₹27,600 crore of index futures over seven trading sessions to November 12. This was a classic short-covering episode, further amplified by substantial actual purchases of shares in the cash market. Of the 50 Nifty companies reporting results, 27 beat analyst estimates. Sales and operating profits rose 22 per cent. Foreign buying is usually concentrated in large, liquid companies, particularly financial stocks, whose weighting in the Nifty gives each rupee of demand an outsize influence. In the first week of November, Shriram Finance rose 16.8 per cent, Bajaj Finance 15.8 per cent, Mahindra & Mahindra 15.7 per cent, HDFC Bank 13.8 per cent, and Reliance Industries 13.3 per cent.  What comes next? A powerful rally after a long period of listlessness can set the stage for a prolonged rise, the reasons for which are sometimes unfathomable. From a deeply pessimistic market in late December 2011, the Nifty staged a remarkable seven-week rally of 21 per cent up to the third week of February 2012, with no clear explanation. It is quite another matter that over the next three months almost all the gains had been wiped out. There is no way to tell whether this is the beginning of another long bull market, particularly if the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz remains unresolved. However, I remain bullish on smaller Indian companies and the domestic fund flows that support them. This is a durable trend which I have highlighted several times this year.

entry.title: Clean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian banking
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Clean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian bankingClean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian banking

As the rate cycle turns, margins should get some relief, but how banks navigate emerging stress in unsecured personal and gold loans remains to be seen

premium

Representative Image

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTWalk into the treasury floor of any bank today, and you’re certain to hear a sigh of relief among dealers. After nearly touching 7.5 per cent in late October, the 10-year benchmark government bond yield is now consolidating between 7.1 per cent and 7.2 per cent.  Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions: When yields rise, bond values fall, triggering a mark-to-market (MTM) hit on banks' treasury income. The country's largest lender, State Bank of India (SBI), saw its treasury income drop about 20 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) in the September quarter, weighed down by both the earlier uptick in bond yields and a depreciating rupee.  A recent report by CareEdge Ratings pegs the fall in treasury income across select scheduled commercial banks in the September quarter at 61.6 per cent y-o-y. Private sector banks saw a 65.7 per cent drop, sharper than their public sector peers at 59.4 per cent. As bond yields hardened towards the end of the quarter, banks were forced to book MTM losses—the notional loss recognised when the market value of securities falls below their book value, even if they are not sold—and had fewer opportunities to book trading profits.  Another pain point is the persistent squeeze in low-cost current account and savings account (Casa) deposits. All listed universal banks reported a y-o-y drop in their Casa ratio, barring five. Three of them are in the public sector (Indian Overseas Bank or IOB, Union Bank of India and Indian Bank) and two in the private sector (Federal Bank Ltd and Karnataka Bank Ltd). For a few, the contraction was 4 percentage points or more. Among the five exceptions, only IOB recorded a rise—albeit marginal—on both a y-o-y and quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) basis.  IDFC FIRST Bank Ltd leads the industry with a Casa ratio of 48.4 per cent, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (46.47 per cent), Central Bank of India (44.65 per cent), IDBI Bank Ltd (43.82 per cent), Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd (41.97 per cent) and IOB (40.71 per cent). No other bank has crossed the 40 per cent mark. Among large lenders, SBI, ICICI Bank Ltd and Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd maintained a Casa ratio of at least 38 per cent each, while Axis Bank Ltd had 36 per cent and HDFC Bank Ltd 31.6 per cent. For some lenders, large inflows of foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits swelled the term deposit base and pulled the ratio down.  Another headache for bankers is the continued compression in net interest margin (NIM)—broadly, the spread between a bank's yield on advances and its cost of funds. Large private sector lenders bore the brunt of this squeeze due to elevated deposit costs, intense competition for retail funds, and the thin margins earned on the FCNR-B deposits mobilised in large volumes during the quarter.  HDFC Bank's NIM fell 11 basis points (bps) y-o-y and 10 bps q-o-q to 3.16 per cent in the September quarter, its lowest on record. ICICI Bank's margin dropped 12 bps y-o-y and 18 bps sequentially to 4.18 per cent. Axis Bank saw a sharper contraction—down 37 bps y-o-y and 10 bps q-o-q to 3.36 per cent. SBI bucked the trend: Its domestic NIM rose 11 bps sequentially to 3.11 per cent. At 2.94 per cent, its whole-bank NIM was down 3 bps y-o-y but up 8 bps q-o-q. One bps is a hundredth of a percentage point.  Subdued treasury income is a cyclical phenomenon—it routinely occurs when yields harden. The persistent erosion in Casa and NIM, however, points to deeper structural shifts. A steady slide in Casa reflects a fundamental change in how Indian savers deploy their money, forcing banks to adapt to higher funding costs as competition intensifies.  Yet one metric on bank balance sheets signals a far more profound structural transformation and underscores how the business of banking is evolving. No prizes for guessing: It is the steady, continuous decline in bad assets.  Just one public sector bank (PSB) currently has a net non-performing asset (NPA) ratio above 0.5 per cent, alongside five private sector lenders. These six banks are Bandhan Bank Ltd (92 bps), IndusInd Bank Ltd (83 bps), Karnataka Bank Ltd (74 bps), DCB Bank Ltd (73 bps), Punjab & Sind Bank (61 bps) and Jammu & Kashmir Bank (51 bps).  What’s more, every listed bank reported a y-o-y drop in net NPAs in the September quarter. All but one—IDBI Bank—recorded a reduction both y-o-y and q-o-q. IDBI Bank reported a net NPA ratio of 17 bps, down from 21 bps a year ago, though marginally higher than 16 bps in the June quarter.  Among the mega-lenders, SBI reported a net NPA ratio of 36 bps, HDFC Bank 37 bps, ICICI Bank 30 bps and Axis Bank 35 bps. South Indian Bank Ltd boasted the lowest net NPA ratio in the industry at 9 bps, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (12 bps), Tamilnad Mercantile Bank Ltd and Indian Bank (14 bps each), and IOB (16 bps).  On gross NPAs, only two lenders kept their ratio below 1 per cent—Tamilnad Mercantile Bank (61 bps) and Karur Vysya Bank Ltd (69 bps). Next came RBL Bank Ltd (102 bps), Kotak Mahindra Bank (104 bps), HDFC Bank (111 bps), Axis Bank (116 bps), IOB (119 bps), and ICICI Bank and Yes Bank Ltd (120 bps each). SBI's gross NPA ratio stood at 139 bps, its lowest in more than two decades.  In absolute terms, PSBs' gross NPAs fell 12.9 per cent y-o-y to Rs 2.31 trillion at the end of September, while private banks saw a 6.7 per cent drop to Rs 1.28 trillion. Across all listed banks, gross NPAs contracted by 10.8 per cent.  On the net NPA front, PSBs recorded a 13.3 per cent drop to Rs 44,092 crore, while private banks logged a 7.7 per cent decline to Rs 34,606 crore. Aggregate net NPAs across all listed banks fell 10.9 per cent.  To put this turnaround in perspective, gross NPAs of all scheduled commercial banks in India (including foreign banks and small finance banks) had peaked at Rs 10.36 trillion in the fourth quarter of FY18, with net NPAs at Rs 5.21 trillion. At that peak, PSBs accounted for Rs 8.96 trillion of gross NPAs—a staggering 14.6 per cent ratio—and Rs 4.54 trillion of net NPAs (8 per cent). Private banks' gross NPAs then stood at Rs 1.29 trillion (4.7 per cent) and net NPAs at Rs 64,380 crore (2.4 per cent).  On most operational metrics today, PSBs are outperforming their private sector peers. Their operating profits grew 17.2 per cent y-o-y in the September quarter, compared with 13.5 per cent for private banks. Total operating profit for all listed banks rose 15.4 per cent to Rs 1.81 trillion. SBI led with Rs 34,226 crore in operating profit, followed by HDFC Bank (Rs 29,483 crore), ICICI Bank (Rs 20,576 crore), Bank of Baroda (Rs 11,430 crore) and Axis Bank (Rs 11,083 crore). No other lender crossed the Rs 10,000 crore mark.  After setting aside Rs 27,271 crore in provisions for bad loans (down 9.1 per cent y-o-y, though up 7.2 per cent sequentially), aggregate net profit for all listed banks rose 20.1 per cent y-o-y to Rs 1.16 trillion. PSBs and private banks ran neck-and-neck in profit growth. Three lenders crossed the Rs 10,000 crore net profit mark: SBI (Rs 23,038 crore), HDFC Bank (Rs 19,510 crore) and ICICI Bank (Rs 14,843 crore).  So far, the run has been remarkable. In a rising interest rate cycle, floating rate loans reprice upward faster than deposits, lifting NIMs. That should ease the margin squeeze in the coming quarters. But how banks navigate the emerging stress in unsecured personal loans and gold-collateralised lending, however, remains to be seen. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. entry.title: India's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signals
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signalsIndia's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signals

The need is to have liquidity and depth in the market

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Ajay TyagiDiya Shah6 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:34 PM ISTIt is good news that the United Kingdom has recognised India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) as a pricing mechanism under its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which takes effect in January next year. The benefit to Indian exporters, however, rests entirely on the carbon price the CCTS produces.  The CCTS, as it exists today, needs much improvement. This column focuses on how to have liquidity and depth in the carbon-trading market so that the scheme throws up the right and credible carbon price.  To begin with, the scheme should ensure that there is sufficient demand for carbon-credit certificates (CCCs) in the market at any given time. All the proposed units in different sectors, as announced under the scheme, should be notified in one go. Apart from building demand, this will improve liquidity in the market. The exclusion of high-emitting sectors such as thermal power, which accounts for roughly 40 per cent of national emission, makes no sense. Further, at present, the scheme sets different targets for greenhouse-gas emission for different units in a sector, based on their past emission levels; the laggards in the past have been given softer targets. This is sure to kill demand, besides being unfair to better-performing units. All this would result in an illiquid market and a weak price, not reflective of the true price. The similar category of units within a sector, based on a criterion like revenue or asset size, should be given the same targets. For instance, the integrated steel plants  of similar production capacity should be given the same targets.More importantly, the targets ought to be ambitious from the very beginning, in line with our emission reduction commitments,  and the MRV (measurement, reporting and verification) framework robust. Going forward, more sectors should be notified under the scheme at the earliest.  Under the scheme, entities performing better than the targets would be entitled to get CCCs, which would be credited in their accounts, free of cost, by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE). Underperforming entities can then purchase the required CCCs in the market from those having them.  On the trading of CCCs, one could perhaps take a leaf out of the highly successful process followed in the stock market, though admittedly CCCs and stocks are different.  Like stock exchanges (SEs), the exchanges on which CCCs would trade (herein after referred to as exchanges) may keep a small window before the start of trading day for call auction to determine the opening price of a CCC. In case there is no participation by entities in the call auction, the previous-day closing price will be the opening price. The closing price will be the volume-adjusted weighted average price (VWAP) derived during the last half an hour of trading in the day. Depending on the level of volatility in trading prices at any given time, the exchanges may prescribe a price band, with the floor and ceiling being a certain percentage of the price. The clearing and settlement mechanism may be through a clearing corporation. There are two suggestions for improving liquidity in the carbon-trading market. The exchanges may introduce a market-making scheme in the first few years of trading. Market makers are financial institutions that simultaneously give “buy” and “sell” quotes to improve liquidity. Of course, they would need to be compensated for the losses incurred by them. SEs have schemes on market making for illiquid stocks, eg stocks for small and medium enterprises. The exchanges could learn from the experience of SEs.  The other suggestion to improve the depth of the market is to introduce derivatives trading for CCCs. The obligated entities could lock in compliance costs by buying futures. Futures prices would give an early signal of where the carbon price is heading. The European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS) shows the scale this can reach. Nearly 90 per cent of allowances trade as futures, and about 65 per cent of secondary-market participants are financial players who typically sell the futures that compliance firms buy to protect themselves against rising prices. South Korea offers what happens in the absence of financial players. With financial participants initially excluded, allowance trading stalled for eight months in 2015, and only 0.06 per cent of allocated allowances changed hands in the first year. After state banks were appointed market makers in 2019 and financial intermediaries were admitted, annual traded volumes rose from 5.66 million tonnes in 2015 to 54.72 million tonnes by 2021.  While the market for CCCs may be regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), the futures market may come under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) like it does for the derivatives market for commodities. A similar arrangement exists for electricity trading. Electricity futures, launched in July 2025, rest on a clear division of roles. The CERC oversees physical power trading on the exchanges, while Sebi regulates futures settled in cash against those exchange prices. A clearing corporation guarantees every contract and collects margins upfront, and protect against defaults. Within their first year, futures volumes on the National Stock Exchange alone reached roughly half the physical day-ahead market, evidence that hedging demand exists once the infrastructure is in place.  The futures on CCCs should trade on  Sebi-regulated exchanges, and settled against the VWAP prices discovered in the physical market. The overall and participant-specific position limits, as a percentage of the trading volumes in the physical market, would need to be put to ensure that the futures market doesn’t manipulate the physical market.  The CCTS begins on a rather tentative note. The scheme was notified in 2023 but trading is yet to start. It is not a good idea to begin the scheme on a weak footing. Any failure would be seen as a non-serious attempt by the government. Except for the suggestions relating to the derivatives market, all other suggestions made above, including allowing financial institutions participation as market makers, may be made part of the scheme right away. The derivatives market may be introduced later at an appropriate time, but the intention to develop it in future should find mention in the scheme now itself so as to give the right message to the world at large about our commitment to develop a credible carbon market in the country. 
The writers are, respectively, former chairman, Sebi, and research assistant, Observer Research Foundation   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Consumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claim
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Consumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claimConsumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claim

The National Commission has held that insistence on a full and final discharge is not justified, as it deprives the insured of their right to take legal action for the balance claim

premium

Policyholders should not sign full and final discharge vouchers if they intend to pursue the balance of their insurance claims.

Jehangir B Gai3 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTLosses suffered by a business can have devastating consequences, not only for the insured but also for its employees and others connected with it. If a business ceases to function, its employees lose their livelihood, while creditors find it challenging to recover the value of goods supplied on credit. Meanwhile, interest and other fixed expenses keep rising, resulting in a crushing financial burden on the insured.  The very purpose of insurance is to insulate a business and safeguard it against unexpected losses. This can happen only if the insurer promptly assesses and settles the claim. Unfortunately, the sad reality is that insurers generally keep claims pending for months. Even when the insurer assesses a claim, it makes several deductions that may or may not be acceptable to the insured.  In cases where the insurer does not pay the full claim, it invariably insists on a full and final discharge before releasing the amount offered. The insured, meanwhile, wants to accept the settlement conditionally, without prejudice to his right to claim the remaining amount that the insurer has disallowed. However, insurers usually capitalise on the insured’s financial predicament and refuse to release the assessed amount, so that they obtain a full and final discharge and the insured forfeits his right to claim the balance. In this column, I will deal with the rights of an insured who finds himself in such a situation.  What does the law say?   The law is well settled that once the insured executes a full and final discharge voucher, he would ordinarily not have the right to claim the balance amount, as the Supreme Court of India held in New India Assurance Co v Genus Power Infrastructure.  An exception to this general rule is permissible only if the insured can establish that he executed the discharge voucher due to coercion, as the Supreme Court of India  laid down in United India Insurance v Ajmer Singh Cotton & General Mills & Ors. Here, the court emphasised that executing discharge vouchers does not inherently prevent policyholders from seeking additional compensation if they can demonstrate that the insurer obtained the vouchers through fraudulent means or undue influence. However, the burden of proof is on the insured, and it is not easy to establish coercion.  The viable remedy  The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has held that such insistence on a full and final discharge is not justified, as it deprives the insured of their right to take legal action for the balance claim. It held that when the insured gives a discharge “under protest”, the insurer must pay the admitted amount, and withholding it would constitute an unfair trade practice. Hence, in K L Malhotra v Oriental Insurance Co Ltd & Anr and Abhay Neelawarne v New India Assurance Co Ltd & Anr, it issued general directions to stop such unfair practices and ordered the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) to issue appropriate instructions.  What should the insured do?  An insured must refuse to execute a full and final discharge if he wants to take legal action to recover the balance claim amount. The remedy lies in filing a consumer complaint and applying for interim relief directing the insurer to release the admitted amount.  The writer is a consumer activist     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: The business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potential
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potentialThe business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potential

Women borrowers are emerging as a key growth driver for lenders, offering higher credit growth, lower delinquencies and significant untapped business potential

premium

India’s next phase of credit growth hinges on how effectively lenders serve women entrepreneurs by designing products for them

Manish Shah4 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 9:24 PM ISTFor decades, access to formal credit has been a powerful engine of economic mobility. In India, one of the most significant developments in the credit ecosystem is the growing presence of women borrowers. What began as a financial inclusion effort has steadily evolved into a compelling economic opportunity for financial institutions.  Women borrowers have over the past five years grown at a compound annual growth rate of 14.2 per cent (compared to 8.2 per cent for men), reaching 89 million by December 2025 and accounting for nearly 28 per cent of the retail credit base, according to CRIF High Mark's March 2026 report called The Credit Goes to Her. Their credit portfolios are expanding faster, with 23.4 per cent year-on-year growth (16.7 per cent for men), while active loans are growing more than twice as fast. This positions women as key drivers of incremental credit demand. Women exhibit lower delinquency rates at 2.8 per cent (3.3 per cent for men). Their role in productive credit is also rising steadily, with secured business loans to women growing over 61 per cent year-on-year and accounting for more than half of loan volumes. Women are also the fastest-growing segment of first-time borrowers, with their share in new-to-credit originations increasing from 33 per cent to 41 per cent in two years.  These trends make a compelling case: Women borrowers offer higher growth, lower risk and long-term value, making them central to the future of lending. The rise of the woman entrepreneur is seen from neighbourhood retail outlets and service businesses to emerging digital ventures. Across sectors and geographies, more women are moving beyond participation and becoming key economic contributors and business decision-makers. This shift is particularly visible in smaller cities and emerging markets, where access to formal finance is enabling women entrepreneurs to scale businesses, generate employment and contribute meaningfully to local economies.  Despite encouraging progress, several structural challenges continue to shape women’s access to credit. Collateral ownership remains limited, with many women lacking formal property titles required for secured lending. Financial awareness and confidence gaps also continue to influence borrowing behaviour, particularly in smaller markets. In addition, digital access gaps persist across certain borrower segments, even as digital lending platforms expand rapidly.  Encouragingly, government initiatives have helped address some of these barriers. Programmes such as the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana have enabled millions of women to access formal credit. Institutional support has also strengthened women-led self-help group networks, helping connect rural borrowers to the formal banking system. These developments reinforce an important principle: When women gain access to formal finance, they use it productively and repay it responsibly.  A critical gap persists between social-sector lending and mainstream commercial finance for women. While microfinance and self-help groups have enabled access to small-ticket credit, many women entrepreneurs struggle to transition into larger, formal lending ecosystems. This creates a “missing middle”, where businesses are too large for microfinance yet not adequately served by traditional banking. As a result, women-led enterprises continue to face a significant financing gap, estimated to be as high as 70 per cent, representing a large untapped opportunity for formal financial institutions.  Bridging this gap will require a shift in how lenders assess and serve women borrowers. Despite demonstrating strong repayment behaviour, women often receive smaller loan sizes and limited access to growth capital. Addressing this calls for more inclusive underwriting models, greater use of alternative data and stronger support systems.  For lenders, the path forward is clear. Women borrowers represent a high-quality credit segment that remains underserved relative to its potential. Financial institutions that invest early in this segment will not only support economic inclusion but also strengthen their own business fundamentals. Designing products tailored for women entrepreneurs, building advisory support mechanisms and expanding outreach can unlock long-term value.  In many ways, the next phase of credit growth will be shaped by how effectively the financial ecosystem engages with women entrepreneurs.
  The writer is the managing director and chief executive officer of Godrej Capital     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: MTNL-BSNL merger needs a fresh review as India's telecom market evolves
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / MTNL-BSNL merger needs a fresh review as India's telecom market evolvesMTNL-BSNL merger needs a fresh review as India's telecom market evolves

MTNL, which has a rich land bank, should not be viewed only as a real-estate play. The land monetisation should lead to a strong merged entity in a competitive landscape

premium

Photo: Shutterstock

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:18 PM ISTMahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd (MTNL), once a valued state-owned telecom-service company, has been in the news for the sale of its land assets. Recently, the Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) on Asset Monetisation recommended for Cabinet approval monetising a fresh tranche of the telco’s surplus land and building assets valued at ₹1,100 crore. While monetising land assets has been an ongoing initiative aimed at reducing the piled up debt of MTNL, which offers services in Delhi and Mumbai, the government must provide clarity on the telco’s future and that of its subscribers. With landline or wireline teledensity (active connections per 100 people) in India at just 3.4 per cent, there’s room for growth in that segment for both calls and the broadband network. In fact, over the past one year or so, there’s been a significant uptick in fixed-phone subscriber numbers, driven by the fibre-to-the-home (FTTH) broadband rollout and growth on the enterprise side. Perhaps, MTNL can still play a constructive role in this space in a timebound manner.  MTNL, which continues to be a listed entity on the stock exchanges, has over the years witnessed erosion in its subscriber base and churn due to its indifferent service quality along with a lack of manpower and resources amid intense competition from the private sector. Even as MTNL is being operated by the unlisted Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd (BSNL) since January 2025 under a service agreement, the much-anticipated merger between the two state-owned telcos was put on hold a few years ago because of MTNL’s financial liabilities, which are estimated at over ₹40,000 crore. While MTNL operates only in Delhi and Mumbai, BSNL is a pan-Indian service provider.  The latest data from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) shows MTNL had only a 2.09 per cent market share in landline-phone connections as of end September. In the same segment, Reliance Jio is on top with 33.06 per cent, followed by Bharti Airtel at 25.46 per cent, Tata Tele at 23.07 per cent, BSNL at 13.67 per cent, Vodafone Idea at 1.57 per cent, and other smaller players holding the remaining market share. The number of landline subscribers in the country increased to 48.74 million at the end of September, from 48.45 million a month earlier, showing a monthly growth rate of 0.60 per cent. In the wireless segment, MTNL is at a 0.01 per cent market share. Jio leads in wireless numbers too with a market share of 39.32 per cent and Bharti Airtel is a close second at 38.02 per cent, while Vodafone Idea is at 15.39 per cent and BSNL at 7.25 per cent. India’s wireless teledensity is estimated at 92.12 per cent.  Since telecom is classified as a strategic sector, the government may not be willing to privatise MTNL. Against that backdrop, the proposal to merge MTNL and BSNL, which has shown signs of operational recovery, though still in losses, should be revived with a definite road map rather than continuing with a service agreement between the two companies, which were telecom heavyweights in the past. MTNL, which has a rich land bank, should not be viewed only as a real-estate play. The land monetisation should lead to a strong merged entity in a competitive landscape.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion Telecom industry MTNL

entry.title: India needs more than production-linked incentives to boost manufacturing
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India needs more than production-linked incentives to boost manufacturingIndia needs more than production-linked incentives to boost manufacturing

Subsidies alone cannot make Indian manufacturing competitive. The assessment makes a clear case for balancing supply-side incentives with demand-side support

premium

Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 11:16 PM ISTThe production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme, introduced in 2020, was intended to address India’s manufacturing disadvantages, attract investment, reduce import dependence, and improve its position in global supply chains. The first comprehensive assessment of the 14 schemes under the PLI, released last week by the NITI Aayog, in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, suggests that the scheme has expanded investment and production, but the impact remains uneven. By March 2026, the scheme had cumulatively attracted ₹2.4 trillion in investment and generated production worth ₹22.66 trillion, achieving 76 per cent and 64 per cent of the respective full-tenure targets. Employment generation, however, stood at just 28 per cent of the target of 3.02 million. As noted in this report, this employment gap needs to be viewed in the context of the gestation period of manufacturing investment. Capital expenditure generally takes place before the factories become fully operational, while production and hiring gather pace as capacity utilisation improves. Nevertheless, the translation of investment into sustainable jobs, particularly in labour-intensive industries, needs closer monitoring.  The export performance offers some encouragement. Cumulative exports reported under the PLI schemes increased from ₹4 trillion in 2023-24 to ₹15.2 trillion in 2025-26. Mobile manufacturing has been a notable success, but much of the activity remains concentrated in final assembly, with continued dependence on imported high-value components. The demand for continued incentives and the recently notified Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme underline the need to deepen domestic capabilities by encouraging technology transfer, greater domestic sourcing, and investment in design and research & development. Progress in other sectors has been slow. Under the advanced chemistry cell battery programme, only 1.4 gigawatt-hour (Gwh) of capacity has been developed against the 50 Gwh target, with commercial production yet to begin. By contrast, the experience of the white-goods sector, where domestic value addition increased from 20 per cent to 55 per cent, shows that deeper localisation is possible.  More broadly, the performance of the PLI schemes needs to be assessed against India’s larger manufacturing ambitions. Despite an increase in manufacturing output, the sector’s contribution to the economy has not registered a sustained rise. Under the revised national accounts series, manufacturing’s share in gross value added at current prices was 14.7 per cent in 2022-23, remained unchanged in 2023-24, declined to 14.5 per cent in 2024-25, and recovered marginally to 14.8 per cent in 2025-26. This suggests that expanding production in select sectors has not yet translated into a significant structural shift in the economy.  Subsidies alone cannot make Indian manufacturing competitive. The assessment makes a clear case for balancing supply-side incentives with demand-side support. Stronger market linkages and export-market development can help create a more reliable market for domestic producers. The focus must also be on strengthening micro, small and medium enterprises, which can supply components and intermediate goods to larger manufacturers. Better access to finance, technology upgrade, workforce skilling, and improvement in testing facilities would help them integrate into domestic and global value chains. The incentives can attract factories, but sustained manufacturing growth will depend on making Indian production more competitive. It is also worth highlighting that the scheme should not take policy attention away from broader reforms. Increasing manufacturing output will need policy reforms in areas like land, labour, capital and trade.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion PLI scheme manufacturing

entry.title: Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boomNvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom

Nvidia clawed its way up from being a specialist in graphics co-processors to become the dominant player in gaming, and then in AI

premium

Nvidia, which was until recently the most valuable company in the world, provides the most crucial component of the hardware infrastructure underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 12:24 AM ISTGlobal stock markets are assessing a situation that management theorists describe as “concentration risk”. The exit of Jensen Huang, who was reportedly honey-trapped, as chief executive officer of Nvidia has created considerable uncertainty about the company’s future. Nvidia, which was until recently the most valuable company in the world, provides the most crucial component of the hardware infrastructure underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom. More broadly, Nvidia holds a dominant market share across the rest of the information technology (IT) industry, and enjoys monopoly status in graphics-intensive spaces such as gaming. Nvidia did not have a succession plan because Mr Jensen did not believe in one. About 60 departments reported directly to him. This may have worked well to accelerate the pace of strategic decisions. But the lack of a formal succession plan means that the Nvidia board must face the challenges of appointing a capable team. That team must develop and articulate a consistent business strategy, and restore investor confidence in a $4 trillion company. Moreover, Nvidia faces investigations from multiple agencies of the United States (US) government and will likely be forced to answer questions in the US Congress. The leadership vacuum has also led Wall Street to suddenly focus on a possible financial weakness in Nvidia’s circular sales strategy. The chipmaker has an excellent credit rating and deploys that to help customers who need to raise debt to buy its chips. The Nvidia balance sheet discloses that it has over $108 billion in outstanding credit guarantees resulting from this circular strategy. One high-profile deal involves selling chips to Oracle, which has debt guarantees from Nvidia. Oracle will use those chips to set up data centres that OpenAI will run. The concentration risks are, therefore, evident. Nvidia holds a dominant share in critical market segments and, if it stumbles operationally, there would be slowdowns across broad swathes of the digital economy. If, in addition, financial issues arise with its guarantees and the circular model blows up, the sums involved are big enough to trigger a crisis across global financial markets. To use an oft-abused phrase, Nvidia may genuinely be too big to fail. And yet, history is not on its side.  It operates in the most hi-tech hardware segment, and no company has maintained dominance for too long in that segment. In prior cycles, IBM, Intel and AMD dominated the chip landscape. Nvidia clawed its way up from being a specialist in graphics co-processors to become the dominant player in gaming, and then in AI. (A co-processor is a chip that runs number-intensive calculations, leaving the main processor in a computer free to do other things.) Google is using its internally designed TPUs (tensor processing units) and intends to start selling and leasing them out. China, officially deprived of access to Nvidia technology, is said to be developing alternatives. But there will be a gap in the market until such alternatives are available in industrial quantities. If Nvidia cannot put a succession plan in place, deal with investigations, sell the succession plan to investors, and navigate the circular financing situation, the exit of one man could result in a cascade of disastrous consequences. The AI bubble is currently deflating, with Nvidia being one of the triggers. If the bubble pops instead of reverting gradually to rational valuations, it could lead to substantial volatility in financial markets if not a full-blown crisis.   Topics : Artificial intelligence Nvidia industry stock markets Global stock markets Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment
